# vibator

Project rules instead of check scripts. A small framework for the checks a
project's linters do not cover, over JavaScript and TypeScript projects.

Read `docs/design/` before changing behavior. Those four files are the contract:
`vibator-namespace.md`, `rule-definition.md`, `configuration.md`,
`command-line.md`. Update the design doc in the same change as the code.

`docs/guide/` holds the guides that vibator.dev publishes for each release.
Update a guide in the same change when its examples or commands change. Links
between docs are relative Markdown links, such as `../design/configuration.md`.

## Layout

```
src/
  namespace/      the `vibator` object a rule reads: project, ts, json, text,
                  ignore, git, shell, package, module, glob. Plus runtime state
                  (root, excludes, scope) and discovery.
  rules/          defineRule and the registry, Rule/Report/Diagnostic/Severity.
                  The package ships no rules.
  configuration/  .vibator.json types, the schema, and load.
  engine/         loadRules and run (the check → fix → check loop). Thin.
  cli/            argument parsing, subcommands, reporters. Calls the engine.
  testing/        runRule, exported as `vibator/testing`.
  cli.ts          the binary.
  index.ts        the public surface.
.vibator/         the rules vibator runs on itself, against the build.
docs/design/      the reference docs.
docs/guide/       the guides, numbered in reading order.
scripts/          build tooling, run through package.json.
```

The public surface (`src/index.ts`) is the namespace, the rule surface, the
configuration types, and the engine. The CLI is the binary, not a library
export.

## Working on it

```sh
npx vitest run                        # the tests
npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json     # the types
npm run generate                      # regenerate schema.json from configSchema
npm run self                          # run this repo's own rules (after build)
npm run docs:format                   # format the Markdown with remark
npm run package                       # publint and attw on the packed package
```

Work test-first, one module at a time: write the test, run it red, write the
code, run it green. Every function gets a test unless it is a trivial re-export.

## Invariants

Do not undo these.

- The engine stays thin. Rules carry the work through the namespace; the engine
  loads rules and runs the check, fix, check loop, nothing more.
- Rules own traversal. A rule reads `vibator.project.files` and decides what to
  walk. The framework imposes no file selection.
- Paths in the namespace are absolute. Reporters relativize for display.
- `defineRule` registers into a map. A duplicate id is an error before any rule
  runs. Importing a rule module registers it.
- The three diagnostic fields stay separate: `message`, `expected`, `fix`.
- The namespace is the only I/O. A rule never touches `fs`, `git`, or the shell
  directly.

## Writing

Documentation, comments, commit messages, and user-facing strings use direct
language.

- Write plain declarative sentences. State the fact, then at most one sentence of
  why.
- No em-dashes. Use commas, colons, parentheses, periods.
- No rambling, aphorisms, or clever turns. No "X is what makes Y"; write the fact
  or "Y because X".
- No idioms or unusual verbs. Name things for what they are. No cute jargon.
- One fact per bullet. Paragraphs of one to three short sentences.
- Reference docs carry no essays. A one-line table entry is the documentation;
  add a section only when asked.
- TSDoc every function, private ones included, with complete `@param` and
  `@returns`. Module headers are one line; no explanatory paragraphs.

# Agent skills

vibator ships three skills for Claude Code and compatible agents:

- `writing-vibator-rules`: write a rule instead of a check script.
- `fixing-vibator-findings`: read a report and resolve its findings.
- `configuring-vibator`: set severities, options, extends, plugins, and excludes.

```sh
npx vibator skills --install   # copy into .claude/skills/
```

The writing skill tells the agent to write a rule before it writes a
`scripts/check-*` file, a test that reads repository files, or a line in
AGENTS.md that nothing checks.

## Agents without skill support

The same material is available from the command line, so any agent can use it:

```sh
npx vibator explain <rule>    # the guideline behind a rule
npx vibator --reporter json   # machine-readable findings
```

Each finding in the JSON report carries its rule id, severity, location, and
the three fields an agent acts on: `message`, `expected`, and `fix`.

# Configuring vibator

`.vibator.json` at the project root is optional. Rules in `.vibator/` run
without it. The field reference is in
`node_modules/vibator/docs/design/configuration.md`, and
`node_modules/vibator/schema.json` validates the file.

## Fields

- `rules`: per-rule overrides, keyed by id. A value is a severity string
  (`"off"`, `"warn"`, `"error"`) or an object `{ severity, options }`.
- `extends`: paths or package names of base configs to inherit, in order. The
  project's own fields apply on top.
- `plugins`: paths or package names of plugin modules. A plugin adds namespaces
  to `vibator`, such as `vibator.i18n`, registers rules, or both.
- `exclude`: directory names to skip during file discovery.
- `$schema`: the schema that validates the file.

## Example

```json
{
  "$schema": "./node_modules/vibator/schema.json",
  "extends": ["@acme/vibator-config/vibator.json"],
  "plugins": ["@acme/vibator-i18n"],
  "rules": {
    "todo-has-ticket": "warn",
    "colors-from-tokens": { "options": { "tokens": "src/styles/tokens.css" } }
  }
}
```

## Rules

- A key under `rules` must name a loaded rule. An unknown id is an error.
- With `extends`, plugins add up, `exclude` replaces the base's list, and rules
  merge by id: the later severity wins and options merge by key.
- Override a base's rule in the project's own `rules`. Do not edit the base
  package.
- Turn a rule off with `"<id>": "off"`. Never turn a rule off to hide a real
  finding; fix the finding instead.

Use when a vibator run reports errors or warnings, or before declaring work done in a repo with a .vibator/ folder."

# Fixing vibator findings

Run vibator with the JSON reporter. The output is built to be acted on:

```sh
npx vibator --reporter json
```

Each finding carries `ruleId` and `severity`, the location (`file`, `line`,
`column`), and three fields with distinct jobs:

- `message`: what is wrong. Read it to locate the problem.
- `expected`: the standard, stated positively. This is the target state.
- `fix`: the concrete next action. Act on this field.

## The loop

1. Run `npx vibator --reporter json`. While iterating, scope to your work with
   `--changed` (uncommitted changes) or `--since origin/main` (the branch's
   diff), and `--only <id>` to focus one rule.
2. Group findings by `ruleId` and work rule by rule. Many findings from one
   rule usually share one cause.
3. Apply the `fix`. When it is not enough, read the guideline with
   `npx vibator explain <id>`. It states why the rule exists and what correct
   code looks like, including the exception policy.
4. If the rule is fixable, `npx vibator --write` runs its fix and rechecks.
   Otherwise edit the code yourself.
5. Re-run until clean. Exit code 0 is done. Warnings do not block, but treat
   them the same in code you touched.

## What not to do

- Never edit `.vibator.json` to make a run pass. No severity downgrades, no new
  excludes, no `off`. The config is the project's standard; changing it is a
  human decision, not a fix.
- Do not restate `message` as a code comment. Fix it.
- Do not blanket-ignore. The escape hatch is for the case where the rule is
  wrong about one specific line:

  ```ts
  // vibator-ignore no-todo-without-ticket: tracked on the roadmap, not a ticket
  const value = read();
  ```

  The marker names the rule id, and a reason is optional but should survive
  review. If you write the same reason three times, stop: the code needs a
  different structure, or the rule's configuration needs a human. Say so.

# Writing a vibator rule

A rule is a module in `.vibator/` that calls `defineRule`. vibator loads every
module at the top of that folder. Put helpers in a subfolder; tests and
declaration files are skipped.

The full contract is in
`node_modules/vibator/docs/design/rule-definition.md` for the rule shape and
`node_modules/vibator/docs/design/vibator-namespace.md` for every namespace
function.

## When to write a rule

Write a rule instead of:

- a script under `scripts/` that walks files and exits with an error,
- a test that reads repository files to check a convention,
- a line in AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md that states a standard nothing checks.

Do not write a rule for what Biome, ESLint, Knip, dependency-cruiser, remark, or
`tsc` already check. Configure those tools instead.

## The rule

```ts
import { defineRule, vibator } from "vibator";

export default defineRule({
  id: "todo-has-ticket",
  title: "TODO comments name a ticket",
  check: () =>
    vibator.text
      .search(vibator.project.files.match("src/**/*.ts"), /\bTODO\b(?![^\n]*[A-Z]+-\d+)/)
      .map((hit) => ({
        ...hit,
        message: "TODO without a ticket",
        fix: "Add the ticket id, or remove the TODO",
      })),
});
```

`id`, `title`, and `check` are required. `check` returns the list of
diagnostics, or `{ diagnostics }`. `severity` defaults to `error`.

Add `docs: ".vibator/docs/<id>.md"` when the standard needs more explanation
than `title`. `npx vibator explain <id>` prints it.

## Read through the namespace

A rule reads everything through `vibator`. It never imports `fs`, runs `git`, or
spawns a process directly.

- `vibator.project.files` is the set of files in scope. Filter it with
  `.match(glob)` (a `!` prefix excludes) and loop with `for...of`, `.map`, or
  `.flatMap`.
- `vibator.text.search(files, pattern)` returns every match across a file set,
  each with `file`, `line`, and `column`. Spread a hit into a diagnostic.
- `vibator.text.lines(file)` and `vibator.text.matches(file, pattern)` scan one
  file.
- `vibator.ts.parse(file)` returns a syntax tree. `.nodes` walks it.
- `vibator.json.parse(file)` and `vibator.json.keys(value)` read JSON.
- `vibator.project.exists(path)` checks a path, including ignored build output.
- `vibator.git` and `vibator.shell.run(command)` reach version control and
  commands.
- A plugin in `.vibator.json` can add more namespaces, such as `vibator.i18n`.
  Use them when present. When several rules need the same reading code, move it
  into a namespace with `defineNamespace` instead of a helper each rule copies.

Paths are absolute. Report `file.path`; the run relativizes it for display.

## Report findings

Each diagnostic keeps three fields separate. Never merge them into one sentence.

- `message`: what is wrong.
- `expected`: the standard.
- `fix`: the next action.

Omit `file` for a finding about the whole project.

## Test the rule

```ts
import { expect, it } from "vitest";
import { runRule } from "vibator/testing";
import rule from "../.vibator/todo-has-ticket.ts";

it("flags a TODO without a ticket", async () => {
  const findings = await runRule(rule, {
    files: { "src/a.ts": "// TODO tidy\n// TODO ABC-12 tidy" },
  });
  expect(findings.map((finding) => finding.line)).toEqual([1]);
});
```

## Fix under `--write`

Add `fix(options, report)` to correct findings. The framework runs
`check`, then `fix`, then `check`, and reports what the last check leaves.
Write files with `vibator.project.write(path, content)`.

## Honor ignore markers

Skip a finding the author opted out of:

```ts
.filter((hit) => !vibator.ignore.line(vibator.project.files.get(hit.file), hit.line, "todo-has-ticket"))
```

A marker reads `vibator-ignore <rule-id>: <reason>` on the line above, or
`vibator-ignore-file <rule-id>: <reason>` anywhere in the file.

## Replace the script

After the rule works, delete the script, its npm script, and its CI step. Run
`npx vibator` where the script ran.

# Accessibility

vibator is a command-line tool. Its interface is the report it prints and its
documentation. Both aim to work with a screen reader, with a screen magnifier,
and without color.

The site at [vibator.dev](https://vibator.dev) has its own
[accessibility statement](https://github.com/vibator/vibator.dev/blob/main/ACCESSIBILITY.md).

## What the command line does

- The report names the severity of each finding as a word, `error` or `warn`. Color is never the only signal.
- `NO_COLOR` turns colors off. `FORCE_COLOR` turns them on when the output is not a terminal.
- The spinner draws only on a terminal. It stays off when `TERM=dumb`, and `--no-progress` turns it off, so a screen reader reads the report alone.
- Each finding starts on its own line with the file, the line, the severity, the rule, and the message.
- `--reporter json` and `--reporter sarif` give the same findings to tools that present them their own way, such as an editor or code scanning.
- Each finding keeps what is wrong, the standard, and the next action in separate fields, in plain words.

## What the documentation does

- Images carry alt text, or `alt=""` when they are decoration.
- Headings do not skip a level.
- Link text names where the link goes.

## How it is checked

- Tests cover the spinner on a terminal, with `TERM=dumb`, and with `--no-progress`.
- The rule `.vibator/markdown-accessible.ts` checks every Markdown file in the repository for alt text, heading levels, and link text. `npm run verify` runs it.

## Known limitations

- The code under each finding has line numbers and a `|` separator, which a screen reader reads aloud. `--reporter json` leaves them out.
- The colors are the terminal's red and yellow. Their contrast depends on the terminal theme.
- The messages are English only.
- VoiceOver, NVDA, JAWS, and Orca have not been tested by hand.

## Report a barrier

[Open an accessibility issue](https://github.com/vibator/vibator/issues/new?template=03_accessibility.yml)
and say what stopped you, with which command, terminal, and assistive
technology. Every report is read. There is no fixed timeline for a fix.

# Contributor Covenant 3.0 Code of Conduct

## Our Pledge

We pledge to make our community welcoming, safe, and equitable for all.

We are committed to fostering an environment that respects and promotes the dignity, rights, and contributions of all individuals, regardless of characteristics including race, ethnicity, caste, color, age, physical characteristics, neurodiversity, disability, sex or gender, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, language, philosophy or religion, national or social origin, socio-economic position, level of education, or other status. The same privileges of participation are extended to everyone who participates in good faith and in accordance with this Covenant.

## Encouraged Behaviors

While acknowledging differences in social norms, we all strive to meet our community's expectations for positive behavior. We also understand that our words and actions may be interpreted differently than we intend based on culture, background, or native language.

With these considerations in mind, we agree to behave mindfully toward each other and act in ways that center our shared values, including:

1. Respecting the **purpose of our community**, our activities, and our ways of gathering.
2. Engaging **kindly and honestly** with others.
3. Respecting **different viewpoints** and experiences.
4. **Taking responsibility** for our actions and contributions.
5. Gracefully giving and accepting **constructive feedback**.
6. Committing to **repairing harm** when it occurs.
7. Behaving in other ways that promote and sustain the **well-being of our community**.

## Restricted Behaviors

We agree to restrict the following behaviors in our community. Instances, threats, and promotion of these behaviors are violations of this Code of Conduct.

1. **Harassment.** Violating explicitly expressed boundaries or engaging in unnecessary personal attention after any clear request to stop.
2. **Character attacks.** Making insulting, demeaning, or pejorative comments directed at a community member or group of people.
3. **Stereotyping or discrimination.** Characterizing anyone's personality or behavior on the basis of immutable identities or traits.
4. **Sexualization.** Behaving in a way that would generally be considered inappropriately intimate in the context or purpose of the community.
5. **Violating confidentiality**. Sharing or acting on someone's personal or private information without their permission.
6. **Endangerment.** Causing, encouraging, or threatening violence or other harm toward any person or group.
7. Behaving in other ways that **threaten the well-being** of our community.

### Other Restrictions

1. **Misleading identity.** Impersonating someone else for any reason, or pretending to be someone else to evade enforcement actions.
2. **Failing to credit sources.** Not properly crediting the sources of content you contribute.
3. **Promotional materials**. Sharing marketing or other commercial content in a way that is outside the norms of the community.
4. **Irresponsible communication.** Failing to responsibly present content which includes, links or describes any other restricted behaviors.

## Reporting an Issue

Tensions can occur between community members even when they are trying their best to collaborate. Not every conflict represents a code of conduct violation, and this Code of Conduct reinforces encouraged behaviors and norms that can help avoid conflicts and minimize harm.

When an incident does occur, it is important to report it promptly. To report a possible violation, email the maintainers at <contact@vibator.dev>.

Community Moderators take reports of violations seriously and will make every effort to respond in a timely manner. They will investigate all reports of code of conduct violations, reviewing messages, logs, and recordings, or interviewing witnesses and other participants. Community Moderators will keep investigation and enforcement actions as transparent as possible while prioritizing safety and confidentiality. In order to honor these values, enforcement actions are carried out in private with the involved parties, but communicating to the whole community may be part of a mutually agreed upon resolution.

## Addressing and Repairing Harm

If an investigation by the Community Moderators finds that this Code of Conduct has been violated, the following enforcement ladder may be used to determine how best to repair harm, based on the incident's impact on the individuals involved and the community as a whole. Depending on the severity of a violation, lower rungs on the ladder may be skipped.

1. Warning
   1. Event: A violation involving a single incident or series of incidents.
   2. Consequence: A private, written warning from the Community Moderators.
   3. Repair: Examples of repair include a private written apology, acknowledgement of responsibility, and seeking clarification on expectations.
2. Temporarily Limited Activities
   1. Event: A repeated incidence of a violation that previously resulted in a warning, or the first incidence of a more serious violation.
   2. Consequence: A private, written warning with a time-limited cooldown period designed to underscore the seriousness of the situation and give the community members involved time to process the incident. The cooldown period may be limited to particular communication channels or interactions with particular community members.
   3. Repair: Examples of repair may include making an apology, using the cooldown period to reflect on actions and impact, and being thoughtful about re-entering community spaces after the period is over.
3. Temporary Suspension
   1. Event: A pattern of repeated violation which the Community Moderators have tried to address with warnings, or a single serious violation.
   2. Consequence: A private written warning with conditions for return from suspension. In general, temporary suspensions give the person being suspended time to reflect upon their behavior and possible corrective actions.
   3. Repair: Examples of repair include respecting the spirit of the suspension, meeting the specified conditions for return, and being thoughtful about how to reintegrate with the community when the suspension is lifted.
4. Permanent Ban
   1. Event: A pattern of repeated code of conduct violations that other steps on the ladder have failed to resolve, or a violation so serious that the Community Moderators determine there is no way to keep the community safe with this person as a member.
   2. Consequence: Access to all community spaces, tools, and communication channels is removed. In general, permanent bans should be rarely used, should have strong reasoning behind them, and should only be resorted to if working through other remedies has failed to change the behavior.
   3. Repair: There is no possible repair in cases of this severity.

This enforcement ladder is intended as a guideline. It does not limit the ability of Community Managers to use their discretion and judgment, in keeping with the best interests of our community.

# Contributing to vibator

Thanks for contributing. This document is for humans. Agents working in this
repository also follow [CLAUDE.md](./CLAUDE.md), and the design invariants
listed there bind all contributions. Participation is governed by the
[Code of Conduct](./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

## Setup

```sh
npm install
npm run verify    # the whole gate: lint, docs, arch, knip, build, package, self, test
```

`verify` runs the whole gate:

| Step                 | Tool                         | Checks                                                      |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm run lint`       | Biome (strict, `biome.json`) | Formatting, lint rules, complexity limits                   |
| `npm run docs:check` | remark (`.remarkrc.mjs`)     | Markdown links and headings                                 |
| `npm run arch`       | dependency-cruiser           | Layer boundaries, cycles, dynamic `typescript`              |
| `npm run knip`       | knip                         | Dead code, unused exports and dependencies                  |
| `npm run build`      | tsc + generate               | Type errors, stale `schema.json`                            |
| `npm run package`    | publint + attw               | The packed package and its type entry points                |
| `npm run self`       | vibator                      | The rules in `.vibator/`: Markdown format and accessibility |
| `npm run test`       | vitest                       | Unit tests, with coverage                                   |

Requirements: Node 24 or later (see `.nvmrc`). Any package manager works, but
CI and the lockfile use npm. Node runs the TypeScript source directly through
type stripping, so there is no build step while developing. `npm run format`
applies Biome's formatting. `npm run docs:format` formats the Markdown, as does
`npx vibator --only markdown-formatted --write` after a build.

`schema.json` is generated from the configuration schema by the build. Commit
the regenerated file when you change the configuration schema. CI fails when it
is out of sync.

## Git hooks

`npm install` installs the hooks (husky):

- **pre-commit**: Biome on the staged files.
- **commit-msg**: commitlint. The commit type sets the release bump.
- **pre-push**: the full `npm run verify`.

## Commits

Conventional Commits, enforced locally and in CI. semantic-release cuts releases
from the commit history, so the type you choose is the version bump you cause:

- `fix:` patch, `feat:` minor, `feat!:` or `BREAKING CHANGE:` major.
- `docs:`, `chore:`, `test:`, `refactor:` produce no release.

Write the subject line for the changelog reader, not the diff reader.

## Changing behavior

The framework ships no rules. A rule lives in a project's `.vibator/` folder or
a plugin package, written against the `vibator` namespace, so rule authoring is
a task for consumers, not this repository. Contributions here change the
namespace, the rule surface, the configuration, the engine, or the CLI.

Read the design docs in [docs/design/](./docs/design/) before changing behavior.
Those four files are the contract. Here is a summary of the design choices:

- The engine is thin.
- Rules own traversal.
- The namespace is the only I/O.
- The three diagnostic fields are separate.
- `typescript` is an optional peer loaded with `await import`.

Update the design doc in the same change as the code, if it is needed.

## Style

- Biome owns formatting and lint.
- dependency-cruiser sets the layer boundaries:
  - `namespace` → imports no other src module
  - `rules` → imports only the `namespace`
  - `configuration` → reads the `namespace`
  - `engine` → imports `namespace`, `rules`, `configuration`
  - `cli` → the root; imports anything, nothing imports it
  - `typescript` → type-only or dynamic import
- knip keeps exports and dependencies in use or gone.

Documentation and user-visible strings (CLI output, rule messages, `fix` texts)
use plain, direct language.

If `npm run verify` passes, the style is right. Do not argue with a check in a
pull request; open an issue instead.

## Pull requests

Keep them scoped to one change. Fill in the template, including the local
verification checklist. CI runs the same `verify` chain plus commit linting. A
pull request merges with a green run and a review from a main contributor.

# Security Policy

## Supported Versions

At any given time we support the _latest_ version of Vibator (as reflected in
the _main_ branch) with security updates.

## Reporting a Vulnerability

If you think you have found a vulnerability, please report it responsibly.
Do not create a GitHub issue for a security problem. Instead, use one of
these channels and we will look into it as soon as we can:

- [Report a vulnerability](https://github.com/vibator/vibator/security/advisories/new)
  privately on GitHub. This is the preferred channel.
- Send an email to <contact@vibator.dev>.

We appreciate any responsible disclosure of vulnerabilities that might impact
the integrity of our users and their projects. We do not offer bounties, but
if you wish we will credit you in the release notes.

Before reporting, make sure you are on the latest version of Vibator and a
supported Node version (22 or later).

# Command line

This document is the reference of the `vibator` command line: the command that
runs the rules, its options, and the subcommands, as they are provided by the
base vibator framework.

## Reference

- [vibator](#vibator): Run every enabled rule.
- [Reporters](#reporters): The output formats.
- [Subcommands](#subcommands): The informational and setup commands.
- [Exit codes](#exit-codes): What the process returns.

---

## vibator

The default command runs every enabled rule.

| Flag                              | Description                                                                                |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| --write                           | Runs each rule's `fix` and rechecks.                                                       |
| --only \<ids>                     | Runs only the comma-separated rule ids.                                                    |
| --config \<path>                  | Loads configuration from a path.                                                           |
| --reporter \<pretty\|json\|sarif> | Chooses the output format. Defaults to `pretty`.                                           |
| --staged                          | Scopes the run to files staged for commit.                                                 |
| --changed                         | Scopes the run to uncommitted changes.                                                     |
| --since \<ref>                    | Scopes the run to changes since a ref.                                                     |
| --no-progress                     | Hides the spinner. It is also hidden when standard error is not a terminal or `TERM=dumb`. |
| --help                            | Prints usage.                                                                              |
| --version                         | Prints the version.                                                                        |

## Reporters

The output formats the `--reporter` flag selects.

| Format | Description                                                                                                       |
| ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| pretty | A readable, colored report for a terminal[^1]. The default.                                                       |
| json   | The machine-readable format, for a direct integration.                                                            |
| sarif  | The [SARIF](https://sarifweb.azurewebsites.net) interchange format, for tools such as trunk.io and code scanning. |

[^1]: Set the `NO_COLOR` environment variable to disable colors, or `FORCE_COLOR`
    to enable them when standard output is not a terminal.

## Subcommands

| Command          | Description                                               |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| list             | Prints every rule with its severity and title.            |
| explain \<rule>  | Prints the guideline for a rule.                          |
| init             | Writes a starter rule, `.vibator/no-conflict-markers.ts`. |
| skills --install | Copies the bundled skills into the project.               |

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning                                            |
| ---- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| 0    | Findings stay at warning severity or below.        |
| 1    | An error-severity finding, or a rule that crashed. |

# `.vibator.json`

This document is the reference of the `.vibator.json` configuration file: the
fields it accepts and the way the framework loads rules, as they are provided by
the base vibator framework.

A project adds a `.vibator.json` at its root. The file is optional and overrides
the default configuration.

## Reference

- [Fields](#fields): The top-level fields of the file.
- [extends](#extends): How a config inherits from base configs.
- [rules](#rules): Per-rule overrides.
- [RuleConfig](#ruleconfig): The override one rule accepts.
- [Loading](#loading): How the framework finds and loads rules.

---

## Fields

The top-level fields of the file.

| Declaration                                                                                     | Description                                                                                                |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| $schema?: string                                                                                | The path or URL of the schema that validates this file.                                                    |
| extends?: string\[]                                                                             | Paths or package names of base configs to inherit, applied in order.                                       |
| plugins?: string\[]                                                                             | Paths or package names of plugin modules. A plugin adds namespaces to `vibator`, registers rules, or both. |
| exclude?: string\[]                                                                             | Directory names to skip during file discovery, replacing the built-in defaults.                            |
| rules?: Record\<string, [Severity](./rule-definition.md#severity) \| [RuleConfig](#ruleconfig)> | Per-rule overrides, keyed by rule id.                                                                      |

## extends

A config inherits each base in `extends`, in order, then applies its own fields
on top. A base can extend other bases. A loop is an error.

| Field   | Merge                                                                                              |
| ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| $schema | Not inherited.                                                                                     |
| plugins | The base's plugins, then the config's own, each once. A base's plugins resolve from the base file. |
| exclude | The config's own list replaces the base's.                                                         |
| rules   | Merged by rule id. For a rule both set, the later severity wins and `options` merge by key.        |

A package base resolves through the package's `exports`, such as
`"extends": ["@acme/vibator-config/vibator.json"]`.

## rules

A rule entry is a [RuleConfig](#ruleconfig). A severity shorthand exists for
convenience: a bare [Severity](./rule-definition.md#severity) stands for that
severity alone, so `{ "no-conflict-markers": "off" }` reads as
`{ "no-conflict-markers": { "severity": "off" } }`.

The framework validates every key against the loaded rules and reports an
unknown rule id as an error.

## RuleConfig

The override one rule accepts.

| Declaration                                          | Description                                             |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| severity?: [Severity](./rule-definition.md#severity) | The severity applied to this rule.                      |
| options?: object                                     | The rule's options, validated by the rule's own schema. |

## Loading

How the framework finds and loads rules.

| Source             | Loading                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `.vibator/` folder | Every `.ts`, `.js`, and `.mjs` module at the top of the folder loads automatically. Tests, specs, declaration files, and subfolders are skipped, so helpers live in a subfolder. |
| `plugins`          | Every module named in `plugins` loads from its path or package, after `.vibator/`. Importing a plugin runs its `defineNamespace` and `defineRule` calls.                         |

Every loaded rule is configured by id in [rules](#rules). Each id stays unique
across the two sources, and the framework reports a repeated id as an error.

# Rule definition

This document is the reference of the rule definition surface: the function
that declares a rule, the shape of a rule, and the types a rule returns, as
they are provided by the base vibator framework. A rule reaches files and
utilities through the [`vibator` namespace](./vibator-namespace.md).

## Reference

- [defineRule](#definerule): Declare a rule.
- [Rule](#rule): The shape of a rule.
- [Report](#report): The result of a rule execution.
- [Diagnostic](#diagnostic): One finding in a report.
- [Severity](#severity): The importance of a finding.
- [runRule](#runrule): Run a rule in a test.
- [Syntax](#syntax): The TypeScript a rule module can use.

---

## defineRule

Declare a rule.

| Declaration                                    | Description                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| defineRule(rule: [Rule](#rule)): [Rule](#rule) | Declares a rule and infers its options type from the schema. |

## Rule

The shape of a rule. `id`, `title`, and `check` are required; the rest carry
defaults.

| Declaration                                                                                                                              | Description                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| id: string                                                                                                                               | The stable kebab-case identifier, used as the config key.                                        |
| title: string                                                                                                                            | One line describing what the rule enforces.                                                      |
| docs?: string                                                                                                                            | The path to the guideline.                                                                       |
| severity?: [Severity](#severity)                                                                                                         | The default severity. The framework applies `"error"` by default.                                |
| options?: ZodType\<Options>                                                                                                              | The schema that validates and defaults the rule's config block.                                  |
| check(options: Options): [Report](#report) \| [Diagnostic](#diagnostic)\[] \| Promise<[Report](#report) \| [Diagnostic](#diagnostic)\[]> | Runs the rule across the files it chooses and returns a report, or the bare list of diagnostics. |
| fix?(options: Options, report: [Report](#report)): void \| Promise\<void>                                                                | Corrects the findings in a report. The framework calls it under `--write`.                       |

`Options` is the type inferred from the `options` schema. A rule that declares
no schema receives an empty options object.

A `docs` value resolves from the project root, such as
`.vibator/docs/my-rule.md`. A rule from a plugin passes an absolute path.

A rule that implements `fix` runs it only when `--write` is enabled. The
framework then drives that rule through a recheck loop, `check` → `fix` →
`check`, and reports whatever findings the final `check` leaves.

## Report

The result of a rule execution. One rule produces one report covering every
file it read.

| Declaration                               | Description                            |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| diagnostics: [Diagnostic](#diagnostic)\[] | Every finding from the rule execution. |

## Diagnostic

One finding in a report.

| Declaration       | Description                                                                                                               |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| file?: string     | The absolute path of the finding; reporters display it relative to the project root. Omit it for a whole-project finding. |
| line?: number     | The start line, or the single line where the finding is.                                                                  |
| endLine?: number  | The last line, when the finding spans several.                                                                            |
| column?: number   | The column where the finding starts.                                                                                      |
| message: string   | What the finding reports as wrong.                                                                                        |
| expected?: string | The standard the rule requires.                                                                                           |
| fix?: string      | The concrete next action that resolves it.                                                                                |

The framework keeps only these fields, so a rule can spread a richer value into
a diagnostic, such as a [Hit](./vibator-namespace.md#hit):
`{ ...hit, message: "..." }`.

## Severity

The importance the framework assigns a finding.

| Value   | Description                                    |
| ------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| "error" | Fails the run.                                 |
| "warn"  | Reports the finding and keeps the run passing. |
| "off"   | Skips the rule.                                |

## runRule

Run one rule against a temporary project in a test. Import it from
`vibator/testing`.

| Declaration                                                               | Description                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| runRule(rule: [Rule](#rule), fixture?: RuleFixture): Promise\<Finding\[]> | Writes the fixture files into a temporary folder, runs the rule, and returns its findings with root-relative paths and no snippet or guideline. |

| RuleFixture field               | Description                                                    |
| ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| files?: Record\<string, string> | The content of each project file, keyed by root-relative path. |
| options?: object                | The rule options, as `.vibator.json` passes them.              |

## Syntax

The TypeScript a rule module can use. The framework loads each rule module with
a plain `import()`, so the runtime compiles it.

| Runtime | Accepts                                                                 |
| ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Node 24 | Erasable syntax only. Enums, parameter properties, and namespaces fail. |
| Bun     | Any TypeScript.                                                         |

A rule that loads on Bun can fail on Node. Write rules with erasable syntax so
they run on both. TypeScript 5.8 and later check this with `erasableSyntaxOnly`
in the `tsconfig` that covers the rules.

---

## External types

Types provided by other packages.

| Type    | Source                 |
| ------- | ---------------------- |
| ZodType | [zod](https://zod.dev) |

## Extending the namespace

A plugin adds a namespace when its module is imported. Rules then read it as
`vibator.<name>`.

| Declaration                                        | Description                                                                               |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| defineNamespace(name: string, value: Value): Value | Adds a namespace to `vibator` and returns it. A name `vibator` already has is an error.   |
| interface Vibator                                  | The type of `vibator`. A plugin adds its namespace to it with `declare module "vibator"`. |

```ts
import { defineNamespace } from "vibator";

export const audit = defineNamespace("audit", { count: () => 3 });

declare module "vibator" {
  interface Vibator {
    audit: typeof audit;
  }
}
```

A rule's file sees the declared type once it imports the plugin's types, such
as `import type {} from "@acme/audit";`.

## Types

The objects returned and accepted across the namespaces above.

### FileSet

An ordered collection of files, with glob filtering and lookup by path. It is
iterable, so a rule can loop over it with `for...of`.

| Declaration                                                               | Description                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| match(glob: string \| string\[]): [FileSet](#fileset)                     | Filters the set to files matching the glob or globs.       |
| get(path: string): [File](#file)                                          | The file at an absolute path.                              |
| length: number                                                            | The count of files in the set.                             |
| forEach(visit: (file: [File](#file), index: number) => void): void        | Runs a function over each file in order.                   |
| map(transform: (file: [File](#file), index: number) => T): T\[]           | Maps each file to a value.                                 |
| flatMap(transform: (file: [File](#file), index: number) => T\[]): T\[]    | Maps each file to a list of values and flattens the lists. |
| filter(keep: (file: [File](#file)) => boolean): [FileSet](#fileset)       | Returns the files that satisfy a predicate.                |
| find(match: (file: [File](#file)) => boolean): [File](#file) \| undefined | Returns the first file that satisfies a predicate.         |
| paths(): string\[]                                                        | The absolute paths in the set, sorted.                     |

# What is vibator?

vibator is a small framework for project rules over JavaScript and TypeScript
projects. It ships no rules. You write a rule as one file in `.vibator/`, and
`npx vibator` runs it, reports its findings, and applies its fix on request.

## The problem it solves

Coding agents check project standards with one-off scripts. Ask an agent to make
sure every locale file has the same keys, and it writes
`scripts/check-locales.mjs` and adds an npm script to run it.

Repeat that for each standard and the project collects a folder of scripts. Each
one has its own file discovery, its own output format, and its own exit code.

A vibator rule replaces one of those scripts. The rule keeps the check.
vibator provides the file discovery, the parsing helpers, the report, and the
command line.

## How it works

- A rule reads the project through the `vibator` namespace and returns its
  findings.
- The namespace covers files, text, JSON, TypeScript, `package.json`, git, and
  the shell.
- A rule decides which files it reads. It sees every file at once, so it can
  compare files with each other.
- Each finding has a `message` (what is wrong), an `expected` value (the
  standard), and a `fix` (the next action).
- A rule can implement `fix`. Under `--write`, vibator runs `check`, then `fix`,
  then `check` again.
- Each rule has a severity: `error`, `warn`, or `off`.
- The output is a terminal report, JSON, or SARIF.

## What a rule is for

A rule covers a check that applies to one project only. For example:

- Every locale file has the keys of the default locale.
- Every environment variable the code reads is listed in `.env.example`.
- Every generated file matches its source.
- CSS colors come from the design tokens.

If a tool you already use has a rule for the check, configure that tool. If the
check would otherwise need a script, write a vibator rule.

# Getting started

## Install

Install vibator as a dev dependency. It requires Node 24 or later, or Bun 1.4.2
or later.

```sh
npm install --save-dev vibator
npx vibator init
```

With Bun:

```sh
bun add -d vibator
bunx --bun vibator init
bunx --bun vibator
```

`--bun` runs the binary on Bun. The binary has a `#!/usr/bin/env node` shebang,
so without the flag `bunx vibator` runs on Node whenever Node is installed. The
`npx vibator` commands in these guides become `bunx --bun vibator`.

`init` writes a starter rule, `.vibator/no-conflict-markers.ts`. It reports
lines left over from a merge conflict.

`typescript` is an optional peer dependency. The `ts` namespace uses the
project's own installation, version 5.4 up to 6.x.

## Write a rule

A rule is a module in `.vibator/` that calls `defineRule`. It reads the project
through the [`vibator` namespace](../design/vibator-namespace.md) and returns
its findings.

```ts
// .vibator/colors-from-tokens.ts
import { defineRule, vibator } from "vibator";

export default defineRule({
  id: "colors-from-tokens",
  title: "CSS colors come from tokens.css",
  check: () =>
    vibator.text
      .search(
        vibator.project.files.match(["src/**/*.css", "!src/styles/tokens.css"]),
        /#[0-9a-f]{3,8}\b/i,
      )
      .map((hit) => ({
        ...hit,
        message: `Hardcoded color ${hit.text}`,
        fix: "Use a variable from tokens.css",
      })),
});
```

`text.search` returns every match across a set of files, each with its `file`,
`line`, and `column`. Spread a match into a finding and add the message.

`id`, `title`, and `check` are required. See the
[rule definition](../design/rule-definition.md) for the full shape.

## Run it

```sh
npx vibator                   # run every rule
npx vibator --write           # run each rule's fix, then check again
npx vibator list              # every rule, its severity, and its title
npx vibator explain <rule>    # the guideline behind a rule
npx vibator --only <ids>      # run only these rules
```

```text
src/components/card.css:11:23 error colors-from-tokens  Hardcoded color #f97316
```

## Test it

`runRule` from `vibator/testing` runs one rule against content you write in the
test. Each entry of `files` is a path and its text:

```ts
import { expect, it } from "vitest";
import { runRule } from "vibator/testing";
import rule from "../.vibator/colors-from-tokens.ts";

it("flags a hardcoded color", async () => {
  const findings = await runRule(rule, {
    files: { "src/card.css": "a { color: #fff; }" },
  });
  expect(findings.map((finding) => finding.message)).toEqual([
    "Hardcoded color #fff",
  ]);
});
```

`runRule` writes the entries into a temporary folder and deletes it after the
run, so the repository holds no broken files.

## Configure the rules

`.vibator.json` at the project root is optional. It sets the severity and the
options of each rule.

```json
{
  "rules": {
    "colors-from-tokens": "warn"
  }
}
```

See the [configuration reference](../design/configuration.md) for every field.

## Adopt on an existing codebase

To check only new work, limit the run to changed files:

```sh
npx vibator --since origin/main   # everything this branch changed
npx vibator --changed             # every uncommitted change
npx vibator --staged              # the files staged for the next commit
```
